Copper Cable: Categories, UTP and Shielded, Conductor Size, Multipair, Coax

Unit 1: Field Planning. Lesson 3 of 52 in INST1 Academy.

A box lands in the staging room with a jacket printed in tiny letters, and the foreman asks what it is. You need to read cable the way a mechanic reads a part number.

Twisted pair

Four pairs of copper wire are twisted together because a twisted pair cancels most of the noise it picks up and most of the noise it makes. Tighter, more even twists carry higher frequencies. That is why a cable's category matters.

Category   Rated frequency   Notes
5e         100 MHz           minimum for new work; 24 AWG typical
6          250 MHz           spline or tight twist controls crosstalk
6A         500 MHz           larger OD, so it fills pathways faster

Construction

  • UTP has no shield and is the common horizontal cable.
  • F/UTP has a foil around all four pairs. S/FTP has foil on each pair and a braid over the whole cable. STP is the general name for a shielded cable. A shield only helps when it is bonded.
  • 23 AWG and 24 AWG: the lower the number, the thicker the wire.
  • Solid conductors run horizontal and punch down on an IDC. Stranded conductors make patch cords, which flex without breaking but lose more signal, so cords stay short.
  • Multipair cable bundles pairs for voice backbone in 25-pair binder groups, each group marked by a colored binder.

Reading the jacket

The print gives the category, the listing (CMP, CMR, CM), the AWG, and footage marks. Use the footage marks to track what you pulled. If the print is missing, treat the cable as unrated.

Coax

RG-6 is the standard 75 ohm cable for video and cable television. RG-59 is older and thinner with more loss, used for short video and camera runs. RG-11 is thick and low loss for long and outdoor runs. Video systems are 75 ohm and radio systems are 50 ohm.

Tip: read the print at both ends of the reel before you cut. A reel that changes category midway is a returned reel.
Exam tip: Category 5e is 100 MHz, 6 is 250 MHz, 6A is 500 MHz; stranded for cords, solid for permanent runs.
Remember
Category sets the frequency, solid wire runs the walls, stranded wire makes the cords, and the jacket print tells you what you are holding.
Deeper explanation

Copper Cable: Categories, UTP and Shielded, Conductor Size, Multipair, Coax, explained slowly

Reading a cable's identity

Every reel has a jacket print that tells you what it is. Learn to read it in a few seconds. A typical print runs along the jacket and repeats every two feet or so.

Print element        Example           What it tells you
Maker and part       (the brand)       who made it
Construction         4PR 23 AWG        four pairs, 23 AWG conductors
Category             CAT 6A            performance level
Listing              CMP               plenum rating
Footage marks        0412 FT           running length on the reel

Why the twists matter

The twist rate of each pair is different on purpose, so no two pairs line up and couple noise to each other. A pair signal travels as a difference between its two wires, and noise that hits both wires equally cancels out. That is why untwisting more than 13 mm (0.5 in) at a termination for Category 5e and above degrades performance.

Matching cable to the job

Job                           Cable choice
Workstation drop              Category 6, solid, UTP
Wireless access point         Category 6A, solid, higher power margin
Patch cord                    Category 6, stranded
Plenum ceiling                same category, CMP jacket
Voice backbone                multipair, 25-pair binder groups
Cable TV drop                 RG-6, 75 ohm

Worked example

You pulled 600 ft of cable from a reel whose footage mark read 2150 at the start. At the end of the pull the mark reads 1550. The footage counts down, so you used 2150 - 1550 = 600 ft. If the print shows a CMR jacket and the job is a plenum ceiling, that cable cannot be used even if the category is right. A higher rating can replace a lower one, never the reverse.

Shielded cable

F/UTP, S/FTP, and other STP cable need a bonded shield. A shielded cable whose shield is left unbonded loses the benefit of the shield and can cause noise problems.

Remember: solid for the wall, stranded for the cord; category sets the frequency; the print tells you the truth.
